chase_cards.name: No.1 Trainer
chase_cards.why: The first-place Secret Super Battle card is the upper step of a regional ladder whose prize text points toward a hidden final battle; it is not just another No.1 Trainer title.

key_artists.name: Hideki Kazama
key_artists.why: Collector and auction references attribute the Secret Super Battle regional Trainer artwork to Hideki Kazama; the credit matters because the card's black Mewtwo silhouette is part of the event's dramatic identity, not a generic trophy frame.

claims.text: The local catalog models the Secret Super Battle regional first place prize as a one-row unnumbered promotional source group containing No.1 Trainer at source index 113.

Bulbapedia's No.1 Trainer page says Secret Super Battle regional copies were awarded to regional champions at Challenge Road '99 SUMMER, with older participants routed to Secret Super Battle rather than Tropical Mega Battle.
Pokumon describes Challenge Road '99 SUMMER as a two-division road: elementary-school players aimed at Tropical Mega Battle, while middle-school and older players aimed at Secret Super Battle.
The Secret Super Battle route is memorable because the card text itself sends winners toward a secret final location, making the trophy card part credential and part invitation story.
Auction and collector references identify Hideki Kazama as the illustrator for the Secret Super Battle regional No.1 Trainer.

Any No.1 Trainer match must preserve Secret Super Battle, Challenge Road '99 SUMMER, senior-division route, source index 113, first-place rank, and Mewtwo-silhouette context before it is treated as this catalog row.

The recurring No.1 Trainer title appears across many Japanese tournament eras, so this release must be separated from Kamex Mega Battle, Tropical Mega Battle, World Challenge Secret Super Battle, Best in Japan, Neo Road, Battle Road, and Worlds trophy cards.

narrative.human_title: Secret Super Battle regional No.1 Trainer: the credential for the hidden room
narrative.why_it_matters: This is the part of early Pokemon Organized Play that feels almost mythic: a child wins through a regional road, receives a card with a dark Mewtwo shape, and the object points them toward a final battle that is deliberately kept mysterious. The card is a trophy, but also a route marker. For agents, the key is to keep that route intact instead of flattening it into the common phrase No.1 Trainer.
